To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Finite-size scaling theory can be applied to practical percolation networks, such as silver nanowire thin films, to predict the minimum size of a device feature that will function; 2) The minimum size is determined by the length distribution of nanowires in the film, which is a function of synthesis conditions; 3) A simple method for predicting the minimum device size from the transmittance-sheet resistivity curve of the film is demonstrated.

finite-size scaling theory can be applied to rod percolation networks such as silver nanowire thin films, to predict a minimum feature size for practical device applications, and that this minimum feature size depends on a combination of the length and aspect ratio distribution of the percollating rods.

the minimum viable feature width of a percolation-based device is related to the length of the longest percolating path in a film by a factor of 1.4, and that the length of the percolation path is related to the transmittance and sheet resistance of a film by a power law with exponent 0.8, which is independent of the length distribution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a fundamental understanding of the scaling properties of nanostructured percolation networks, and how this knowledge can be used in practical device applications.
understanding the behaviour of percolating systems at finite size, and the application of this understanding to the development of practical devices.
the design and fabrication of silver nanowires for use in touch sensing applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the finite-size scaling theory of percolation is a powerful and useful tool for the design and optimisation of nanostructured electrode systems, and that this theory is applicable to a wide range of practical systems.
finite-size scaling theory is applicable to practical percolating systems, and that it is a valuable tool for the design of devices which rely on percolation networks.
finite-size scaling theory is an essential tool for understanding and designing practical devices from percolating networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

finite-size scaling theory is applicable to practical percolation systems such as silver nanowire electrode films, and can be used to derive a design rule relating feature size to length distribution of the material.
we have demonstrated a method for the design of practical AgNW electrodes, based on the finite-size scaling of the percolated networks.
we have developed a design rule for patterning silver nanowire networks for use in capacitive touch sensing applications.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the scaling behaviour of a percolating network of nanorods is determined by the distribution of the lengths of the rods, and not the distribution of the diameters, and that this behaviour can be understood and quantified using simple finite-size scaling theory.
, for any given rod percolation system, there is a critical length distribution which will result in the best possible scaling properties.
, in contrast to conventional wisdom, the performance of AgNW electrodes in such applications is not necessarily limited by the minimum feature size of the pattern.
